Question 1

calculator

medium

[Maximum marks: 17]

Mass spectra and line spectra can reveal details about the structure and composition of elements.

  1. The mass spectrum of bromine gas is shown below.

    1. Calculate the relative molecular mass of bromine gas using the mass spectrum and exact isotope masses of 157.84, 159.83, and 161.83 m/zm/zm/z in the calculation. Give your answer to two decimal places. [3]

    2. For the species with the peak at m/z=79,m/z = 79,m/z=79, state the number of neutrons, protons, and electrons. [2]

     \ \newline  # of neutrons   \ \newline \   \qquad \qquad \qquad
     \ \newline  # of protons\textbf{\# of protons}# of protons   \ \newline \   
     \ \newline  # of electrons\textbf{\# of electrons}# of electrons   \ \newline \   

    \mbox{}\\[-10pts]

  2. The electron configuration and position on the periodic table can reveal information about the element.

    1. State the condensed electron configuration of a bromine atom. [1]

    2. Describe what information can be deduced about the electron configurations of fluorine and chlorine, given that they are in the same group as bromine. [1]

    3. Explain, with a reason, the trend observed in electronegativity in the halogens. [2]

  3. Line spectra reveal information about the electronic structure of atoms.

    1. Explain how the hydrogen emission spectrum provides evidence for the existence of discrete energy levels in atoms. [2]

    2. Describe what the limit of convergence represents in terms of electron transitions. [1]

  4. Bromine participates in radical reactions such as the halogenation of alkanes.

    \mbox{}\\[-15pts]

    1. State whether the cleavage of a Br−Br\ce{Br-Br}Br−Br bond in the initiation step is homolytic or heterolytic. Illustrate the reaction by drawing the bond fission with arrows showing the movement of electrons. [2]

    2. The average Br−Br\ce{Br-Br}Br−Br bond enthalpy is 193 kJ mol−1.193 \textrm{\ kJ mol}^{-1}.193 kJ mol−1. Calculate the wavelength, in nm,\textrm{nm},nm, of light required to break a Br−Br\ce{Br-Br}Br−Br bond in the gas phase. [3]

Question 2

calculator

medium

[Maximum marks: 25]

Trimethylamine, (CHX3)X3N,\ce{(CH3)3N},(CHX3​)X3​N, is a monobasic amine used industrially in the synthesis of herbicides and dyes.

  1. Trimethylamine has a base hydrolysis constant Kb=6.5×10−5K_b=6.5\times10^{-5}Kb​=6.5×10−5 at 298 K.

    1. Write an equation for the equilibrium between aqueous trimethylamine and water. [1]

    2. Deduce the molecular geometry and approximate bond angle around the nitrogen atom in (CHX3)X3N\ce{(CH3)3N}(CHX3​)X3​N and its conjugate acid. [4]

    \qquad shape \qquad\qquad bond angle \qquad
     base \ \newline \qquad \textbf{base}\qquad \newline \  base 
     acid \ \newline \qquad \textbf{acid}\qquad \newline \  acid 

    \mbox{}\\[-20pts]

  2. Calculate the pH of a 0.150 mol dm−30.150 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}0.150 mol dm−3 solution of N(CHX3)X3.\ce{N(CH3)3}.N(CHX3​)X3​. [3]

  3. 20.0 cm320.0 \textrm{\ cm}^320.0 cm3 of 0.150 mol dm−30.150 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}0.150 mol dm−3 trimethylamine is titrated with 0.100 mol dm−30.100 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}0.100 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid. Sketch the pH curve for this titration on the axes provided. [3]

  1. Explain the difference in the ability of trimethylamine and methylpropane to form complexes with transition-metal ions. [2]

  2. The industrial formation of trimethylamine occurs by the reaction

    \mbox{}\\[-25pts]

    3 CHX3OH+NHX3⟶(CHX3)X3N+3 HX2OΔH=−175 kJ mol−13 \ce{\,CH3OH} + \ce{NH3} \longrightarrow \ce{(CH3)3N} + 3 \ce{\,H2O}\qquad \Delta H = -175 \textrm{\ kJ mol}^{-1}3CHX3​OH+NHX3​⟶(CHX3​)X3​N+3HX2​OΔH=−175 kJ mol−1

    \mbox{}\\[-25pts]

    1. Explain, using collision theory, why the rate of this reaction increases when the temperature is raised.[3]

    2. Sketch an energy profile diagram for this reaction, with and without a catalyst. Clearly label the curves. [3]

    3. Equal 0.100 mol dm−30.100 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}0.100 mol dm−3 solutions of methanol and ammonia are mixed. On the axes provided, sketch concentration−-−time curves for CHX3OH\ce{CH3OH}CHX3​OH and NHX3.\ce{NH3}.NHX3​. [2]

  3. Trimethylamine can be oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to form trimethylamine N−-−oxide (TMAO): \mbox{}\\[10pts]

    (CHX3)X3N(aq)+HX2OX2(aq)⟶(CHX3)X3NO(aq)+HX2O(l)\ce{(CH3)3N}\textrm{(aq)} + \ce{H2O2}\textrm{(aq)} \longrightarrow \ce{(CH3)3NO}\textrm{(aq)} + \ce{H2O}\textrm{(l)}(CHX3​)X3​N(aq)+HX2​OX2​(aq)⟶(CHX3​)X3​NO(aq)+HX2​O(l)

    \mbox{}\\[-15pts]

    1. Deduce the oxidation state of nitrogen in (CH₃)₃N and in TMAO. [2]

    2. Write the balanced oxidation and reduction half reactions for the reaction above in acidic conditions. [2]

Question 3

calculator

medium

[Maximum marks: 25]

Butan−-−1−-−ol is used in the cosmetic industry and can be produced from 1−-−chlorobutane.

  1. Draw the full structural formula of 1−-−chlorobutane. [1]

  2. Butan−-−1−-−ol belongs to the homologous series of alcohols.

    1. State three features of a homologous series. [3]

    2. Deduce the general formula of alcohols. [1]

  3. Write a balanced chemical equation for the conversion of 1−-−chlorobutane into butan−-−1−-−ol and identify the nucleophile and leaving group. [3]

  4. The carbon in the C−Cl\ce{C-Cl}C−Cl bond acts as an electrophile. Explain this behaviour. [2]

  5. Draw the transition state for this mechanism. [2]

    1. Name a structural isomer of butan−-−1−-−ol that is a secondary alcohol. [1]

    2. Draw the stereoisomers of the secondary alcohol named in part (f)(i), using wedge−-−dash representation. [2]

    3. One stereoisomer of 2−-−butanol rotates plane−-−polarized light by +13.52°.+13.52\degree.+13.52°. Predict the observed rotation of its mirror image. [1]

  7. Another isomer of butan−-−1−-−ol is given below.

    Comment on the number of 1^11H NMR signals, their integration ratios, and their splitting patterns expected in this spectrum. [3]

  8. The IR spectrum of butan−-−1−-−ol shows a broad absorption that is not present in 1−-−chlorobutane. Identify the bond responsible and state the approximate wavenumber range for this absorption. [2]

  9. The mass spectrum of butan−-−1−-−ol shows a molecular ion peak at m/z=74m/z = 74m/z=74 and another peak at m/z=31.m/z = 31.m/z=31. Identify the species responsible for each peak. [2]

  10. Samples of 1−-−iodobutane and 1−-−chlorobutane of the same concentration are hydrolysed under identical aqueous conditions. State and explain which which reacts faster.[2]

medium

[Maximum marks: 23]

Water can be electrolysed to produce hydrogen gas, an energy carrier that can be used as a fuel:

\mbox{}\\[-15pts]

2 HX2O(l)⟶2 HX2(g)+OX2(g)2\ce{\,H2O}\textrm{(l)} \longrightarrow 2\ce{\,H2}\textrm{(g)} + \ce{O2}\textrm{(g)}2HX2​O(l)⟶2HX2​(g)+OX2​(g)

  1. The diagram shows a Hofmann voltameter that uses platinum electrodes and dilute NaX2SOX4(aq)\ce{Na2SO4}\textrm{(aq)}NaX2​SOX4​(aq) to electrolyse water, producing HX2(g)\ce{H2}\textrm{(g)}HX2​(g) and OX2(g),\ce{O2}\textrm{(g),}OX2​(g), after electrolysis has been occurring for some time.

    1. Label the anode and the cathode and show the direction of electron flow. [2]

    2. State the role of sodium sulfate in this electrolysis. [1]

    3. Phenolphthalein is added to the central reservoir. Using Section 18 of the IB Chemistry data booklet, describe and explain the colour changes observed near each electrode during the electrolysis. [2]

    4. During the experiment, 22.5 cm322.5 \textrm{\ cm}^322.5 cm3 of HX2(g)\ce{H2}\textrm{(g)}HX2​(g) are collected at 100 kPa100 \textrm{\ kPa}100 kPa and 298 K.298 \textrm{\ K}.298 K. Calculate the number of electrons that have passed through the circuit to produce this volume of hydrogen gas. [3]

  2. The voltage required for the electrolysis of water can be determined using standard thermodynamic values.

    1. Using Section 13 of the IB Chemistry data booklet, calculate the standard enthalpy and change, ΔH⦵,\Delta H^{\minuso},ΔH∘−, in kJ mol−1,\textrm{kJ mol}^{-1},kJ mol−1, and entropy change, ΔS⦵,\Delta S^{\minuso},ΔS∘−, in J K−1 mol−1,\textrm{J K}^{-1}\textrm{\,mol}^{-1},J K−1mol−1, for the reaction: 2 HX2O(l)⟶2 HX2(g)+OX2(g).2\ce{\,H2O}\textrm{(l)} \longrightarrow 2\ce{\,H2}\textrm{(g)} + \ce{O2}\textrm{(g)}.2HX2​O(l)⟶2HX2​(g)+OX2​(g).

      ΔS⦵(OX2)=205.1 J K−1 mol−1,\Delta S^{\minuso}\ce{(O2)} = 205.1 \textrm{\ J K}^{-1}\textrm{\,mol}^{-1},ΔS∘−(OX2​)=205.1 J K−1mol−1, ΔS⦵(HX2)=130.7 J K−1  mol−1\Delta S^{\minuso}\ce{(H2)} = 130.7 \textrm{\ J K}^{-1}\textrm{\, mol}^{-1}ΔS∘−(HX2​)=130.7 J K−1 mol−1 [3]
      \mbox{}\\[-15pts]

    2. From your values in (i), calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, ΔG⦵,\Delta G^{\minuso},ΔG∘−, in kJ mol−1,\textrm{kJ mol}^{-1},kJ mol−1, at 298 K298 \textrm{\ K}298 K and state whether this reaction is spontaneous. [2]

    3. Calculate the minimum cell potential, in V,\textrm{V},V, required for this electrolysis to occur under standard conditions. [3]

  3. An alternative approach to calculating enthalpy changes uses bond dissociation enthalpies, which can provide insights into the role of intermolecular forces. \mbox{}\\[10pts]

    1. Use the bond dissociation enthalpies from Section 12 of the IB Chemistry data booklet to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction: 2 HX2O(g)⟶2 HX2(g)+OX2(g).2\ce{\,H2O}\textrm{(g)} \longrightarrow 2\ce{\,H2}\textrm{(g)} + \ce{O2}\textrm{(g)}.2HX2​O(g)⟶2HX2​(g)+OX2​(g). [3]

    2. Draw a diagram showing all of the hydrogen bonds that one water molecule can form when surrounded by other water molecules in liquid water. [2]

    3. Compare your answer from part (c)(i) with your answer from part (b)(i). Use this comparison to quantitatively estimate the strength of a hydrogen bond in liquid water. [2]
